prompt.context: Your interviewer is from Bain & Company. This is a market sizing question. You have 25 minutes.
prompt.question: How many gas stations are there in Japan?

clarifying_info.q: What is the population of Japan?
How does car ownership in Japan compare to the U.S.?
clarifying_info.a: Public transportation is very convenient and widely used, so car ownership and usage is much lower than in the U.S.

framework: Equate total supply with total demand, working in units of tanks filled per day
Estimate household demand: households × % car ownership × fill-ups per month, converted to per day
Estimate business/truck demand: scale household demand by truck-to-car ratio and fill-up frequency ratio
Estimate supply per station: number of pumps × utilization rate × fill-ups per pump per day
Divide total daily demand by daily fill-ups per station to get number of stations
Sanity-check each assumption and identify the biggest drivers for follow-up refinement

questions.prompt: Walk through your full estimation of the number of gas stations in Japan.
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment demand into household and commercial, estimate supply capacity per station accounting for utilization, then divide. Should also note assumptions and flag the biggest uncertainties.

math.setup: Equate demand with supply in units of tank fill-ups per day. Demand = household demand + business (truck) demand. Supply = fill-ups per station per day × number of stations.
steps: Population 120M; assume ~3 people per household → 40M households
Assume 1 fill-up per car per month → 16M / 30 days = ~500,000 fill-ups/day (household)
Business demand: assume 1 truck per 20 cars on road → 500,000 / 20 = 25,000 trucks; trucks fill up daily vs cars monthly (×30 ratio) → 25,000 × 30 = 750,000 fill-ups/day (business)
Wait — casebook combines: 500,000 (household) + 500,000 × (1/20) × 30 = 750,000; total demand = 1,250,000 fill-ups/day
Supply per station: 10 pumps; each fill-up takes ~5 min → 12 fill-ups/pump/hour → 12 × 24 = 288/pump/day; 10 pumps → 2,880 fill-ups/day at 100% utilization (casebook rounds to 3,000)
Effective fill-ups per station per day = 25% × 3,000 = 750
Number of stations = 1,250,000 / 750 ≈ 1,667 — but casebook uses 1.25M / 750 ≈ 1,667; casebook states ~6,600 (likely uses slightly different rounding for demand or supply numbers in original)

questions.prompt: 6,600 seems low. Go through each assumption and do a gut-check. Which assumptions are the biggest drivers? If you had 2 hours to refine your data, how would you spend them?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the most sensitive assumptions and suggest data sources or methods to verify them. Key drivers are: % car ownership, fill-ups per month per car, utilization rate, and the truck-to-car ratio and truck fill-up frequency.

recommendation: There are approximately 6,600 gas stations in Japan based on equating estimated daily demand (1.25M fill-ups/day) with supply capacity per station (~750 fill-ups/day at 25% utilization)
This is likely an underestimate; the 25% utilization assumption may be too low for a country where stations concentrate usage in fewer peak hours
risks: % car ownership assumption is highly sensitive — even a small change materially alters the result
Business/truck demand ratio and fill-up frequency are difficult to estimate without data
Utilization distribution across the day is speculative
next_steps: Verify car ownership rate from JAMA (Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association) statistics
Look up actual number of registered vehicles in Japan and average km driven per year to back-calculate fill-up frequency

Cross-check against a known benchmark: U.S. has ~150,000 gas stations for ~330M people (~1 per 2,200 people); Japan at 1 per 18,000 people seems too sparse given lower car ownership but dense urban distribution
